f*cking insane. i gave Claude Fable 5.2 one job: "build me an app i can charge for." then gave another AI one rule: "break it before my first customer pays."

my test case: a booking app. pick a slot, pay, get a confirmation.

easy when i'm the only person clicking.

now two people want the last slot. one pays, the confirmation never arrives, and they hit retry.

what just happened to their money?

the part worth stealing: write down what must stay true BEFORE asking AI to find bugs.

for this app:
→ one slot can only belong to one confirmed buyer
→ retrying a payment must never charge twice
→ a successful payment must end in a booking or a refund

then give your coding agent this:

"Turn these rules into a test plan. Try to violate each one with simultaneous users, lost responses and retries. For every scenario, show the exact steps and what should happen."

that second AI is @brekenai.

Fable builds the app. Breken runs the actual software in an isolated environment, fills it with synthetic users and agents, and introduces the failures your happy-path demo never sees.

when it confirms a bug, you get the exact sequence that caused it and a draft fix to review. something you can reproduce, fix and test again before a paying customer hits it.

that's the loop:

try to break a rule → reproduce the failure → review the fix → run the same scenario again → decide what ships

honestly the replay is what i'd pay for. i want to see the SAME checkout that failed survive after the fix. a fresh demo where nobody hits retry tells me nothing.

i want the app to have its worst day while every customer is still fake.

steal the prompt for your own app. then put it through Breken before your paying customers become the test team.

virals.name: Rohan Paul
virals.text:
New Google DeepMind paper shows prompt injection is not solved, since a swarm of strong AI attacker agents still tricks even the best-defended models.

Prompt injection means hiding instructions in data an AI agent reads, like a tool result, to make it act for the attacker. Human red-teaming attacks now almost never work on recent Gemini models, so the problem can look solved.

They built Agentic Optimizer, 8 teams of AI agents that test injections, share notes, and build on each other's best attempts. They tested it on 100 tool-use tasks where the attacker only wanted one random, harmless tool call.

With up to 320 tries, the strongest attacker beat Gemini 4 Argon, the most robust model, on 34% of tasks. Open-weight Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash resisted only 1% of tasks.

United Airlines to Block AI Agents From Booking Flights in Its Website or Third-Parties—Is This For Security? | Isaiah Richard, Techtimes

The idea of letting an AI assistant handle everything from finding flights to completing the booking has been gaining traction with AI developers and consumers alike, but not every business in the travel industry is on board with it.

One of the biggest names in American aviation, United Airlines, has just drawn a firm line.

United Airlines to Block AI Agents From Booking Flights

United Airlines has announced it is updating its ticketing policies to restrict AI agents from booking flights through its website, third-party travel agencies, and flight aggregators. The airline joins a growing list of companies, including JPMorgan Chase and Amazon, that have moved to block AI agents from their platforms over security and privacy concerns.

United laid out several specific reasons for the restriction. When a customer hands an AI agent access to their account to complete a booking, that agent can potentially expose payment information, login credentials, and loyalty account details, leading to what the airline described as unintended purchases, account changes, or unauthorized use of MileagePlus miles.

The company also pointed to a risk unique to air travel: passengers must personally acknowledge that their baggage does not contain hazardous materials during check-in, a legal obligation that only a human being can satisfy.

United CEO Scott Kirby was direct about the company's reluctance to embrace agentic commerce during a public appearance this week. "To be honest, I do not want to create another middleman," Kirby said, articulating a concern that AI agents sitting between United and its customers could erode the direct relationship the airline has built through its own app, website, and loyalty program.

Transportation Department, FAA Also Against AI Agents

Beyond United's own business concerns, the airline specifically cited existing federal regulations from the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration as reasons why AI agent bookings raise compliance problems that go beyond corporate preference, said Engadget.

The FAA and DOT have regulations governing the interaction between airlines and passengers during the booking and check-in process, some of which explicitly require a human acknowledgment or disclosure. The baggage declaration issue is the clearest example: existing rules require the person checking in to personally confirm that their bags do not contain prohibited items. An AI agent completing check-in on a customer's behalf cannot satisfy that legal requirement.

United's concern about AI agents potentially running afoul of these regulations reflects a broader regulatory uncertainty around agentic AI in contexts where consumer protection and safety rules assume a human is making the transaction. As AI agents become more capable, the question of whether a purchase or acknowledgment made autonomously by an AI on a consumer's behalf meets the same legal standard as one made by the consumer directly is likely to become an active question for regulators across the travel industry and beyond.

Some Airlines Still Allow AI Agent Flight Booking

Not every airline is responding to the AI agent question the same way United is. Southwest Airlines took the opposite approach on October 6 when it announced the launch of a first-of-its-kind US airline plugin in ChatGPT, allowing travelers to discover and shop for Southwest flights directly through the AI assistant.

Southwest described the plugin as the first step in a phased AI-powered booking approach developed in partnership with OpenAI and Amazon Web Services. The experience is designed to let travelers move from inspiration and discovery into booking options with Southwest from within a ChatGPT conversation, reducing the number of steps between deciding to travel and completing a purchase.

"Customers are evolving how they plan their travel, and Southwest is helping to shape what comes next," said Sabrina Callahan, Chief Digital and Marketing Officer at Southwest Airlines. The plugin is built to allow Southwest to appear earlier in the customer journey and offer a more direct path from intent to booking, with the airline viewing the AI-assisted channel as a way to reach customers where they are already searching.

The difference in approach between United and Southwest illustrates that there is no industry-wide consensus on how to handle agentic commerce in travel. United sees AI agents as a security and regulatory risk that creates an unwanted layer between the airline and its customers.

Southwest sees the same technology as an opportunity to reach customers earlier in the planning process.

The idea of letting an AI assistant handle everything from finding flights to completing the booking has been gaining traction with AI developers and consumers alike, but not every business in the travel industry is on board with it.

One of the biggest names in American aviation, United Airlines, has just drawn a firm line.

United Airlines to Block AI Agents From Booking Flights

United Airlines has announced it is updating its ticketing policies to restrict AI agents from booking flights through its website, third-party travel agencies, and flight aggregators. The airline joins a growing list of companies, including JPMorgan Chase and Amazon, that have moved to block AI agents from their platforms over security and privacy concerns.

United laid out several specific reasons for the restriction. When a customer hands an AI agent access to their account to complete a booking, that agent can potentially expose payment information, login credentials, and loyalty account details, leading to what the airline described as unintended purchases, account changes, or unauthorized use of MileagePlus miles.

The company also pointed to a risk unique to air travel: passengers must personally acknowledge that their baggage does not contain hazardous materials during check-in, a legal obligation that only a human being can satisfy.

United CEO Scott Kirby was direct about the company's reluctance to embrace agentic commerce during a public appearance this week. "To be honest, I do not want to create another middleman," Kirby said, articulating a concern that AI agents sitting between United and its customers could erode the direct relationship the airline has built through its own app, website, and loyalty program.

Transportation Department, FAA Also Against AI Agents

Beyond United's own business concerns, the airline specifically cited existing federal regulations from the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration as reasons why AI agent bookings raise compliance problems that go beyond corporate preference, said Engadget.

The FAA and DOT have regulations governing the interaction between airlines and passengers during the booking and check-in process, some of which explicitly require a human acknowledgment or disclosure. The baggage declaration issue is the clearest example: existing rules require the person checking in to personally confirm that their bags do not contain prohibited items. An AI agent completing check-in on a customer's behalf cannot satisfy that legal requirement.

United's concern about AI agents potentially running afoul of these regulations reflects a broader regulatory uncertainty around agentic AI in contexts where consumer protection and safety rules assume a human is making the transaction. As AI agents become more capable, the question of whether a purchase or acknowledgment made autonomously by an AI on a consumer's behalf meets the same legal standard as one made by the consumer directly is likely to become an active question for regulators across the travel industry and beyond.

Some Airlines Still Allow AI Agent Flight Booking

Not every airline is responding to the AI agent question the same way United is. Southwest Airlines took the opposite approach on October 6 when it announced the launch of a first-of-its-kind US airline plugin in ChatGPT, allowing travelers to discover and shop for Southwest flights directly through the AI assistant.

Southwest described the plugin as the first step in a phased AI-powered booking approach developed in partnership with OpenAI and Amazon Web Services. The experience is designed to let travelers move from inspiration and discovery into booking options with Southwest from within a ChatGPT conversation, reducing the number of steps between deciding to travel and completing a purchase.

"Customers are evolving how they plan their travel, and Southwest is helping to shape what comes next," said Sabrina Callahan, Chief Digital and Marketing Officer at Southwest Airlines. The plugin is built to allow Southwest to appear earlier in the customer journey and offer a more direct path from intent to booking, with the airline viewing the AI-assisted channel as a way to reach customers where they are already searching.

The difference in approach between United and Southwest illustrates that there is no industry-wide consensus on how to handle agentic commerce in travel. United sees AI agents as a security and regulatory risk that creates an unwanted layer between the airline and its customers.

Southwest sees the same technology as an opportunity to reach customers earlier in the planning process.

outsiders.name: Rohan Paul
outsiders.text:
New Google DeepMind paper shows prompt injection is not solved, since a swarm of strong AI attacker agents still tricks even the best-defended models.

Prompt injection means hiding instructions in data an AI agent reads, like a tool result, to make it act for the attacker. Human red-teaming attacks now almost never work on recent Gemini models, so the problem can look solved.

They built Agentic Optimizer, 8 teams of AI agents that test injections, share notes, and build on each other's best attempts. They tested it on 100 tool-use tasks where the attacker only wanted one random, harmless tool call.

With up to 320 tries, the strongest attacker beat Gemini 4 Argon, the most robust model, on 34% of tasks. Open-weight Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash resisted only 1% of tasks.

United Airlines to Block AI Agents From Booking Flights in Its Website or Third-Parties—Is This For Security? | Isaiah Richard, Techtimes

The idea of letting an AI assistant handle everything from finding flights to completing the booking has been gaining traction with AI developers and consumers alike, but not every business in the travel industry is on board with it.

One of the biggest names in American aviation, United Airlines, has just drawn a firm line.

United Airlines to Block AI Agents From Booking Flights

United Airlines has announced it is updating its ticketing policies to restrict AI agents from booking flights through its website, third-party travel agencies, and flight aggregators. The airline joins a growing list of companies, including JPMorgan Chase and Amazon, that have moved to block AI agents from their platforms over security and privacy concerns.

United laid out several specific reasons for the restriction. When a customer hands an AI agent access to their account to complete a booking, that agent can potentially expose payment information, login credentials, and loyalty account details, leading to what the airline described as unintended purchases, account changes, or unauthorized use of MileagePlus miles.

The company also pointed to a risk unique to air travel: passengers must personally acknowledge that their baggage does not contain hazardous materials during check-in, a legal obligation that only a human being can satisfy.

United CEO Scott Kirby was direct about the company's reluctance to embrace agentic commerce during a public appearance this week. "To be honest, I do not want to create another middleman," Kirby said, articulating a concern that AI agents sitting between United and its customers could erode the direct relationship the airline has built through its own app, website, and loyalty program.

Transportation Department, FAA Also Against AI Agents

Beyond United's own business concerns, the airline specifically cited existing federal regulations from the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration as reasons why AI agent bookings raise compliance problems that go beyond corporate preference, said Engadget.

The FAA and DOT have regulations governing the interaction between airlines and passengers during the booking and check-in process, some of which explicitly require a human acknowledgment or disclosure. The baggage declaration issue is the clearest example: existing rules require the person checking in to personally confirm that their bags do not contain prohibited items. An AI agent completing check-in on a customer's behalf cannot satisfy that legal requirement.

United's concern about AI agents potentially running afoul of these regulations reflects a broader regulatory uncertainty around agentic AI in contexts where consumer protection and safety rules assume a human is making the transaction. As AI agents become more capable, the question of whether a purchase or acknowledgment made autonomously by an AI on a consumer's behalf meets the same legal standard as one made by the consumer directly is likely to become an active question for regulators across the travel industry and beyond.

Some Airlines Still Allow AI Agent Flight Booking

Not every airline is responding to the AI agent question the same way United is. Southwest Airlines took the opposite approach on October 6 when it announced the launch of a first-of-its-kind US airline plugin in ChatGPT, allowing travelers to discover and shop for Southwest flights directly through the AI assistant.

Southwest described the plugin as the first step in a phased AI-powered booking approach developed in partnership with OpenAI and Amazon Web Services. The experience is designed to let travelers move from inspiration and discovery into booking options with Southwest from within a ChatGPT conversation, reducing the number of steps between deciding to travel and completing a purchase.

"Customers are evolving how they plan their travel, and Southwest is helping to shape what comes next," said Sabrina Callahan, Chief Digital and Marketing Officer at Southwest Airlines. The plugin is built to allow Southwest to appear earlier in the customer journey and offer a more direct path from intent to booking, with the airline viewing the AI-assisted channel as a way to reach customers where they are already searching.

The difference in approach between United and Southwest illustrates that there is no industry-wide consensus on how to handle agentic commerce in travel. United sees AI agents as a security and regulatory risk that creates an unwanted layer between the airline and its customers.

Southwest sees the same technology as an opportunity to reach customers earlier in the planning process.
